Surat al-Muzzammil

Meccan in its entirety according to al-Hasan, Ikrimah, 'Ata' and Jabir. Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah said, as al-Mawardi mentioned, that two verses of it are Meccan: ﴿Bear patiently what they say﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 10] and the one that follows it. It is related in al-Bahr from the majority that the surah is Meccan except for His saying ﴿Indeed your Lord knows﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 20] to the end. Al-Jalal al-Suyuti criticized this after quoting the exception from the report of Ibn al-Furs, saying: "It is refuted by what al-Hakim narrated from 'A'ishah, that this was revealed a year after the revelation of the beginning of the surah, at the time when the night prayer was made obligatory at the beginning of Islam, before the five daily prayers were prescribed. What relates to this will come, God willing." Its number of verses is eighteen according to the last of the Medinan (reckoners), nineteen according to the Basran, and twenty according to the others.

When He, glory be to Him, concluded Surat al-Jinn with the mention of the messengers, peace be upon them, He, exalted and majestic, began this surah with what relates to their Seal, upon him and upon them be peace. This is one aspect of the connection, and in Tanasuq al-Durar (the harmony of pearls) the connection of its beginning, ﴿Stand [in prayer] the night﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 2] etc., with His saying at the end of that surah, ﴿And when the servant of God stood calling upon Him﴾ [al-Jinn: 19], and with His saying, glory be to Him, ﴿And that the mosques are for God﴾ [al-Jinn: 18], is not hidden.

(In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful)

Al-Akhfash said: ﴿O you who wraps himself﴾ means al-Mutazammil, from tazammala with his garments, when he wrapped himself in them; so the ta' was assimilated into the za'. Ubayy read it in its original form, and Ikrimah read al-Muzammil with the z lightened and a kasrah on the m, meaning "the one who wraps his body or himself." Some of the early generation read al-Muzamal with the z lightened and a fathah on the m, as a passive participle. There is no contradiction among the readings, for he, upon him be blessings and peace, did indeed wrap himself in his noble garment, without doubt. But if one considers that all his actions are from God, then God wrapped him. There is no need to say that he, upon him be blessings, first wrapped himself, then slept and was wrapped by another; or that another wrapped him first, then what he was wrapped in fell from him, and he wrapped himself.

The majority hold that when the angel came to him in the cave of Hira' and conversed with him as he conversed, he returned to Khadijah, may God be pleased with her, and said, "Wrap me, wrap me." Then ﴿O you who covers himself﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 1] was revealed, and right after it ﴿O you who wraps himself﴾ was revealed.

Al-Bazzar, al-Tabarani in al-Awsat, and Abu Nu'aym in al-Dala'il narrated from Jabir, may God be pleased with him, who said: "When Quraysh gathered in Dar al-Nadwah they said, 'Name this man with a name by which people will turn away from him.' They said, 'A soothsayer.' They said, 'He is not a soothsayer.' They said, 'A madman.' They said, 'He is not a madman.' They said, 'A sorcerer.' They said, 'He is not a sorcerer.' They said, 'He separates the beloved from his beloved.' So the polytheists dispersed on that. This reached the Prophet (ﷺ), so he wrapped himself in his garments and covered himself with them. Then Jibril, peace be upon him, came to him and said, 'O you who wraps himself! O you who covers himself!'"

His (ﷺ) being addressed with this is an act of intimacy and tenderness, in accordance with the custom of the Arabs of deriving a name for the addressee from the attribute that he has. As when he (ﷺ) said to 'Ali, may God honor his face, when he was angry with Fatimah, may God be pleased with her, and he came to him while he was sleeping with dust clinging to his side: "Get up, Abu Turab (father of dust)." This is intended to lift the veil and fold up the carpet of reproach, and to energize him so that he receives what comes to him without sluggishness:

"And everything the beloved does is beloved."

Al-Zamakhshari claimed that he (ﷺ) was addressed with this in order to mock the state he was in, of wrapping himself in a cloak, and his readiness for heavy sleep, as one does who is not concerned with a matter and whose affairs do not trouble him, and so on through what he said. Most scholars said this was a case of bad manners, and some who agreed with him concurred in part. The author of al-Kashf said: "He meant that he (ﷺ) was described with what he was engaged in, reminding him of his lounging. So it is gentle reproach mixed with pure compassion, and it is to energize him and make him ready for what God promised him by His saying, glory be to Him, ﴿Indeed We will send down upon you a weighty word﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 5]. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) is not above such an address, for he was addressed with something harsher in ﴿He frowned and turned away﴾ ['Abasa: 1]. Such address of familiarity and tenderness does not diminish the goodness and closeness within it, compared with ﴿O Prophet﴾ [al-Anfal: 64] and others, nor with ﴿O Messenger﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 41, 67], which carry honor and welcome." End of quotation.

It is not hidden that the bad manners of al-Zamakhshari in his expression are not removed by this. For although He may address His beloved with whatever He wills, we do not act in the way He treated him; rather, respect and honor for his noble presence are required of us. If one of the subjects addressed a vizier with what the sultan addressed him with, the chamberlains would expel him, and perhaps punishment would be the response.

It was also said that he (ﷺ) was wrapped in a striped cloak of 'A'ishah, may God be pleased with her, while praying, so he was called thus as praise and to beautify his state. The command that follows, to stand, does not contradict this, either because it is a command to persist in that and remain constant in it, or it is teaching him (ﷺ) and clarifying the amount he should stand, as has been said. Yes, it was objected to this that the surah is among the first revealed in Mecca, while the Messenger (ﷺ) consummated his marriage with 'A'ishah only in Medina, although the sound reports are abundant that the mentioned address took place while he (ﷺ) was in the house of Khadijah. From this one can know the status of what was narrated from 'A'ishah: she was asked what his tazmil (wrapping) was, and she said, "It was a striped cloak, its length fourteen cubits, half of it over me while I was sleeping and half over him while he was praying. Its warp was hair and its weft was wool."

The author of al-Kashf undertook to answer this, saying: "The answer is that he (ﷺ) contracted the marriage in Mecca, so perhaps the cloak came to him after the contract. Yes, it indicates that it was after the death of Khadijah. The difficulty lies in 'A'ishah's saying 'half of it over me,' etc. Its answer is that it is possible that he spent a night in the house of al-Siddiq, may God be pleased with him, once, and the cloak was over 'A'ishah while she was a little girl, and the rest, because of its length, was over the Prophet (ﷺ). So the Mother of the Believers related that, since there is no indication that it is a narration of what happened after the consummation." This is what is elaborated to validate this view. End.

You know that this hadith did not occur in the sound books, as Ibn Hajar said; rather, it contradicts them. And such possibilities are not sufficient. Indeed, Abu Hayyan said it is a clear lie.

From Qatadah: the Prophet (ﷺ) had wrapped himself in his garments for prayer and prepared himself for it, so he was called, "O you who wraps himself," meaning, "O you who prepares himself for worship." Ikrimah said: the meaning is, "O you who is burdened" by prophethood and its responsibilities. Ziml (burden) is like himl (load) in wording and meaning; it is said izdamalahu, meaning he bore it. In this there is a comparison of carrying out the protocols of prophethood to bearing a heavy load, for both involve hardship. It is permissible that it is a metaphor for one who is sluggish due to lack of habituation, and an objection similar to that raised against al-Zamakhshari's view was raised against it. With the soundness of the literal meaning, and its support by the sound hadiths, there is no need for any other meaning, as has been said.

﴿Stand [in prayer] through the night﴾, that is, stand up to prayer. It was also said that it means to persist in it. Whichever is meant, the object of ﴿قُمِ﴾ is implied. ﴿وَاللَّيْلَ﴾ (*al-layl*, "the night") is in the accusative as an adverb of time (*al-zarfiyya*, the accusative of time or place). It was permitted that it be accusative by way of extension (*al-tawassu'*, broadening of usage) and metaphorical attribution (*al-isnad al-majazi*, attributing an action to something other than its true agent). This view is attributed to the Kufan grammarians, and what was said about the Basran grammarians is the opposite. It was also said that *qiyam* (standing) is used metaphorically for prayer, so the meaning of "قُمِ" is "pray" (*ṣil*), and there is therefore no implied object.

Abu al-Sammal read the *mim* of "قُمِ" with a *damma*, following the vowel of the *qaf*. It was also read with a *fatha*, seeking lightness. The majority reading uses a *kasra*, according to the basic rule for the meeting of two consonants with sukun (*iltiqa' al-sakinayn*). ﴿إلا قَلِيلا﴾ (*illa qalilan*, "except a little") is an exception from ﴿اللَّيْلَ﴾.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 73, verse 3:

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿half of it﴾ is a substitute (badal) for ﴿a little﴾, a substitution of the whole (badal al-kull), and the pronoun refers to the night. In this substitution there is the removal of ambiguity. And in the mention of "a little" there is an indication that the half that is filled with the remembrance of God, Exalted is He, is in the rank of the whole, and that the empty half, although it equals it in quantity, does not equal it in reality. ﴿Or reduce from it﴾ is a conjunction (ʿatf) upon the preceding command, and the pronoun in "from it" also refers to the night, restricted by the exception, because it is the thing the speech was brought for. It was said that it refers to the half because of its proximity. ﴿A little﴾, that is, a small reduction or a small amount, such that it does not fall below half of the half.

[Page 103]

﴿Or add to it﴾ is a coordination (ʿatf) as previously mentioned, and the discussion of the pronoun (ḍamīr) is the same. The meaning does not differ according to the two opinions about it, namely that it is his (ﷺ) being given the choice between standing half the night, or less than half, or more. However, he preferred the first, because in it the measure of decrease and increase is the half that accompanies the standing (qiyam), and this is better than making it the half that is entirely free of standing, even if they are equal in quantity. Some of them were unaware of the substitution (ibdal) from the night remaining after the exception (istithnāʾ), and of the two pronouns referring to it, and said that the substitution from qalīlan is not sound for this reason. Also, what truly deserves attention, which the substitution indicates, is the remaining part after the exception that accompanies the standing, not the excluded part that is free of it. It is not hidden that this is near to complete.

Likewise, Abu Hayyan objected to that substitution, saying: the pronoun in ﴿نِصْفَهُ﴾ (nisfahu, "half of it") in that case either refers to the substituted item (mubdal minhu) or to the item from which the exception is made (mustathnā minhu), which is (al-layl, "the night"). It cannot refer to the substituted item, because that would be an exception of an unknown from an unknown, since the sense would be "except a little, half of the little," and this has absolutely no meaningful sense. Nor can it refer to the item from which the exception is made, because then the exception would be superfluous (laghw). For if it were said, "Stand the night, half of it, or decrease from it a little, or add to it," it would convey the same meaning in a shorter, clearer way, further from ambiguity. In response, we choose the second. As for his claim of superfluity, we have already indicated how to answer it. One of the eminent scholars clarified this by saying: it contains an indication of easing and facilitating the standing, since the smallness of one of the two halves entails the smallness of the other; and an indication of the difference between what is occupied with obedience and what is free of it, implying that the part occupied with it is equivalent to the whole. Along with this is the clarification after ambiguity, which prompts firm retention in the mind and increases eagerness.

As-Samin also criticized the first part, saying that "an exception of an unknown from an unknown" is incorrect, because "the night" is known, and likewise its part, half of it, and what is less or more than it. There is no harm in excepting the unknown from the known, such as ﴿Then they drank from it, except a few﴾ (2:249). Indeed, there is no harm in substituting an unknown for an unknown, like "a group of people came to me, some of them on foot." Nevertheless, what was previously stated is what is relied upon.

It is permissible that ﴿نِصْفَهُ﴾ be a substitute for ﴿اللَّيْلَ﴾, a partial substitution (badal baʿḍ min kull), with the exception made from it, and the speech being according to the intention of inversion (taqdim wa taʾkhir). The original would be: "then half the night, except a little." The pronouns in "from it" and "upon it" refer to the lesser of the half, understood from the whole of the item from which the exception is made. So it is as if it were said: "Stand less than half the night, by standing a third of the night; or decrease from that lesser a little, by standing a quarter of the night; or add to that lesser, by standing half." Thus the choice here is between the lesser of the half and the lesser of the lesser. Otherwise, it is increased from it, which is precisely the half, and its outcome is a choice between the half, the third, and the quarter. It is said that the difference between this aspect and what was mentioned is as clear as the dawn.

In al-Kashshaf there is something that may be understood from it, according to what has been said: that the choice lies beyond the half, i.e., in what is less than half and more than a third, so that by addition one does not reach half, nor by reduction a third. Al-Kashf said: he made the addition less than half and the reduction more than a third because, if they reached a whole fraction, it would have been more appropriate to state them by their explicit names. Also, the preference for "little" (qilla) a second time is an indication of approximation to that lesser, and what reaches a whole fraction is not a little reduction in the sense of this context. And this is said regarding the side of addition; how so, when he based the matter on its being less than half. End of quote. This is a forced view, and in my opinion, what I have heard of its kind is similar to it. The apparent sense of some scholars' words is that mention of the third, the quarter, and the half is by way of example, not that the less, the lesser, and the more are restricted to what was mentioned.

It is also permissible for the speech to be according to the intention of inversion, as mentioned a moment ago, but with the two pronouns referring to the half, not to the lesser of it, as in that view. The meaning is a choice between two matters: between standing, peace be upon him, less than half the night definitively, or choosing one of two matters, namely decrease from the half or increase over it. So it is as if it were said: "Stand less than half the night definitively, or decrease from the half, or add to it, as a choice." It has been said that the lesser is given importance because it is the basic obligation, so it is repeated, like "Honour either Zayd, or Zayd, or ʿAmr." This has been criticized as forced, because placing the exception before the substitution apparently indicates that the substitution is from what remains after the exception, and assuming a postponement of the exception is a departure from the basic arrangement without evidence.

Also, on this view, the apparent reading is that the two pronouns refer to the half after the exception, since it is the one preceding, not the unqualified half. Also, the apparent reading is that reduction is a concession (rukhsa), since addition is voluntary (nafl), and giving priority to the matter of the firm obligation (ʿazīma) is better. Furthermore, on this view it is not permissible to stand for half the night, and the established reading of the seven canonical readings refutes this: ﴿Indeed your Lord knows that you stand [in prayer] for nearly two-thirds of the night, or half of it, or a third of it﴾ (73:20), with the genitive case (jarr). If one argues from the permissibility of the lesser to its permissibility by implication (mafhum al-muwafaqa), it would follow that one must also disregard the mention of addition over half for the same reason. It is not hidden that some of this is objected to in the view mentioned a moment ago. His statement that "the apparent reading is that reduction is a concession" was also objected to as open to question, since the apparent reading is that it belongs to the kind of ﴿And if you complete ten, it is from you﴾ (28:27), so the choice is not in its literal sense. There is discussion in this.

It is also permissible that the substitution is from the second ﴿قَلِيلا﴾ (qalīlan), in the sense of half of the half, which is the quarter, and the pronoun in "upon it" refers to this little. The addition to this little, i.e., the quarter, is made half of the quarter. It is as if it were said: "Stand half the night, or decrease from the half a little, half of it, or add to this little a little, half of it." Its outcome is: "Stand half the night, or half of it, or add to half of the half, half of the half of the half." So the choice, when the night is, for example, sixteen hours, is between standing eight hours, four hours, and six hours. It is not hidden that the unqualified phrasing in "or add to it" apparently indicates that it is not restricted by "a little," since if it were for the sake of economy, then in "or decrease…" and so on, one would have sufficed with the first as well. From here it has been said that the addition, being unqualified, may be taken as completing the third, so the choice is between the half, the third, and the quarter. In reply: making it complete the third has no evidence except agreement with the reading in the genitive in "half of it and third of it," stated later.

The Imam (Fakhr al-Din al-Razi) permitted that qalīlan in ﴿except a little﴾ be intended as a third, and said that nisfahu is by omission of the coordinating particle, so it is as if it were said: "two-thirds of the night, or stand half of it, or decrease from the half, or add to it." He extended his explanation and defense of this, yet its status is not hidden. He also mentioned a second aspect, whose matter is not hidden from one who has comprehensively known what preceded. Yes, his explanation of "little" as a third is narrated from al-Kalbi and Muqatil, and from Wahb ibn Munabbih that it means less than a tenth and a sixth, which, by what we mentioned earlier, is half.

Those who hold that exception of half or more is permissible used this verse as evidence, as detailed in the principles of jurisprudence (usul). Al-Tabrizi said: the command to stand and the choice in addition and reduction fell upon the two-thirds of the latter part of the night, because the first third is the time of ʿatama (the late evening prayer period), and the exception bears on the commanded act. So it is as if it were said: "Stand two-thirds of the night, except a little," then he made nisfahu a substitute for qalīlan, so that qalīlan became explained as half of the two-thirds, which is "little" according to what was mentioned. Or: "decrease from it," i.e., from the commanded act, which is standing two-thirds, a little, i.e., less than half of it. Or: "add to it." Thus the choice in addition and reduction fell upon the two-thirds. End of quote. This is, as you see, [unconvincing].

It has been said that the exception is from the numbers (aʿdad) of the night, not from its parts, because its definiteness is for totality (istighraq), since there is no prior reference. The pronoun refers to it in terms of its parts. Moreover, there is istikhdam (using a word in one sense and a pronoun for it in another) or something similar. The choice is between standing half, less than it, and more than it, and this is far-fetched.

In summary, the exegetes have said much about this verse, to the point of mentioning what is not fitting to derive from the speech of the Mighty God. The clearest view to me, the furthest from artificiality, and most suited to the eloquence of the revelation is what we mentioned first. And God the Exalted knows best what is in His Glorious and Abundant Book.

What relates to the command in His words ﴿Stand [in prayer] the night…﴾ and ﴿recite the Qur'an…﴾ will come, God willing. That is, during the standing mentioned, recite it slowly and deliberately, with clear articulation of the letters, ﴿تَرْتِيلا﴾ (tartīlan, "measured, distinct recitation"), eloquently, such that the listener is able to count them. From their saying: ثَغْرٌ رَتْلٌ (thaghrun ratlun), with the tāʾ sukūn, and رَتِلٌ (ratilun), with the kasra, when the mouth is مُفَلَّجًا (mufallaj, having gaps between the teeth), its teeth not joined to one another.

Al-ʿAskari narrated in al-Mawaʿiz, from ʿAli (may God ennoble his face), that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was asked about this verse, and he said: "Make it clear with clarification, do not scatter it like the scattering of inferior dates (al-daql), and do not rush through it like poetry. Stop at its wonders, move hearts with it, and let not the concern of any one of you be the end of the surah."

﴿Indeed, We shall send down upon you﴾, that is, We shall reveal to you. The choice of the word "casting" (*ilqa'*) here is because of His words ﴿a heavy word﴾, which is the Great Qur'an. Because of the arduous obligations it contains, it is heavy upon those who are charged with them, especially upon the Messenger (ﷺ), for he, peace and blessings be upon him, is commanded to bear them and to convey them to the community. This emphasized sentence is parenthetical (*mu'taridah*) between the command to stand (in prayer) and its subsequent reason, to ease what was imposed upon him, peace and blessings be upon him, of standing in prayer. It is as if it were said: "Indeed, there will come upon you in the revelation sent down difficult obligations; compared to them, this (standing in prayer) is easy. So do not be concerned with this hardship, and train yourself for what follows." Some have included in the parenthetical insertion the clause ﴿and recite the Qur'an distinctly﴾, and so on.

It has been objected that there is no basis for this. It has also been said that the meaning of its being ﴿heavy﴾ is that it is firm (*rasin*), because its structures are sound and its meanings robust. The intended sense is that it surpasses everything else in wording and meaning. But "heavy" is used figuratively for "superior," because being superior is by nature such a quality. Within this meaning is what has been said: the intended sense is speech that has weight and excellence, not something base. It has also been said that its meaning is that it is heavy upon the one who reflects on it, because it requires greater purification of the inner self and concentration of the mind. Thus "heavy" is metaphorical for "difficult." It has also been said that it is heavy in the balance (on the Day of Judgment), and "weight" is either literal or metaphorical for the abundance of reward of its reciter. Abu al-'Aliyah and al-Qurtubi said: its heaviness is upon the disbelievers and the hypocrites, through its inimitability and its warning. It has also been said: "heavy" refers to its reception, meaning that it is heavy upon him (ﷺ), and the revelation of it through the angel is heavy. For revelation came to him, peace and blessings be upon him, in several modes, among them that the angel does not take a form to him and address him, but rather there comes upon him, peace and blessings be upon him, something like a swoon, due to the intense drawing of his noble spirit toward the Exalted Assembly (*al-Mala' al-A'la*), such that he hears what is revealed to him and sees it and perceives it, while he alone, peace and blessings be upon him, perceives it, not those who are with him. In this state he felt a heaviness in his body, so much so that his thigh (ﷺ) nearly crushed the thigh of Zayd ibn Thabit, while it was upon his thigh when revelation came to him.

Ahmad, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Nasr and al-Hakim narrated, and he authenticated it, from 'A'ishah: "When revelation came to the Prophet (ﷺ) while he was on his she-camel, she would lower her chest (*juran*) and could not move until he was relieved of it," and she recited: ﴿Indeed, We shall send down upon you a heavy word﴾.

Al-Shaykhan (al-Bukhari and Muslim), Malik, al-Tirmidhi and al-Nasa'i narrated from her that she said: "I saw him when revelation descended upon him on a very cold day, and it would be released from him, and his forehead would be dripping with sweat."

On this interpretation it is permissible that ﴿heavy﴾ be an adjective of a verbal noun that has been omitted and replaced, taking its accusative position: that is, a heavy casting (*ilqa'an thaqilan*), and not an adjective of "word." It has also been said that this (heaviness) refers to its remaining through the ages, because what is heavy by nature remains in its place.

It has also been said that its heaviness is in terms of the weight of its letters, literally, in the Preserved Tablet (*al-Lawh al-Mahfuz*). Thus it is reported from some of them that every letter of the Qur'an in the Tablet is greater than Mount Qaf, and that if the angels gathered to lift a single letter they could not bear it, until Israfil, peace be upon him, who is the angel of the Tablet, comes and lifts it and carries it by the permission of Allah the Exalted, not by his own strength, but Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has granted him that ability. This needs a sound transmission from the Truthful one (ﷺ), peace and blessings be upon him, and I do not think it exists.

The sentence, according to most of these interpretations, is said to be a new sentence (*mustanifah*) giving the reason, for night prayer (*tahajjud*) prepares the self to cope with its heaviness. So reflect.

The verse has been cited as evidence that it is not proper to say "a light surah," since Allah the Exalted named the entire Qur'an in it ﴿a heavy word﴾. This is a matter of caution, as is not hidden.

﴿Indeed, the rising of the night﴾: that is, the soul that rises from its bed to worship, i.e., rises up. It is said that *nasha'a* (نشأ) means he rose from his place and got up when he stood up, and he recited the verse of poetry:

*We rose to camels with sunken flanks, whom the night-journey wore thin, and from them rose the heights of the hump-tops.*

The apparent meaning of the words of the linguists is that *nasha'a* in this sense is an Arabic usage. Al-Kirmani, in his commentary on al-Bukhari, said it is an Abyssinian (Ethiopic) usage that the Arabs arabicized. A group of scholars narrated something similar from Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Mas'ud, and Abu Hayyan related it from Ibn Jubayr and Ibn Zayd. He took *nashi'a* (ناشئة) as the plural of *nashi'* (ناشئ), as if he meant the rising souls, i.e., the standing ones. The singular form is clear. The annexation (*idafa*) is either in the sense of *fi* ("in"), or of the type of *sayyid ghaḍḍiyy* (a lord of the [tribe of] Ghaḍḍ), and this is more eloquent; or the standing of the night is such that *nashi'a* is a verbal noun of *nasha'a* in the sense of "stood," like *al-'aqiba* (the consequence), and attributing it to the night is a metaphor (*majaz*, figurative usage), as one says: "he stood through his night" and "he fasted through his day." Mujahid restricted this standing to standing up from sleep, and so did 'A'isha, and she refused that it means standing in general. That was because the annexation to "night" in the phrase "standing of the night" conveys standing up from sleep during it, or standing at the time of sleep, for one who says the night is entirely [sleep]. Or the worship that arises, i.e., occurs, at night, where the annexation is specifying (*ikhtisasiyya*), or in the sense of *fi*, or of the type of ﴿the scheming of the night﴾ [Saba': 33]. Ibn Jubayr, Ibn Zayd and a group said: ﴿ناشئة الليل﴾ means its hours, because they arise, i.e., occur, one after another, i.e., successively, and the annexation in this case is specifying. Or its first hours, from *nasha'a*, when it means he began. Al-Kisa'i said: *nashi'a* means its beginning. Close to this is what has been narrated from Ibn 'Umar, Anas ibn Malik and 'Ali ibn al-Husayn, may God be pleased with them all, that it is what lies between the Maghrib and the 'Isha' prayers.

﴿It is firmer in treading﴾: that is, it alone, unlike the rising of the day, is firmer in *muwata'a* (conformity of heart and tongue); its heart conforms with its tongue if by *nashi'a* is meant the soul performing tahajjud (night prayer). Or the heart of the one standing conforms with his tongue in it, if by it is meant the standing or the worship or the hours. The attribution is literal on the first reading, and on this [reading] it is figurative. Considering the implicit metaphor (*isti'ara makniyya*, a metaphor in which the comparison is implied rather than stated) is not so [strong]. Or [it is firmer] in agreement with what is intended of sincerity (*ikhlas*); so there is no figurative usage on all the meanings.

Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn al-Zubayr, Mujahid, and the two Arab readers (Ibn 'Amir and Abu 'Amr) read *wiṭa'an* (وِطاءً) with a kasra on the waw and a fatha on the ta', with a long vowel (*mamdudan*), as the verbal noun of *wata'a*, *wiṭa'an*, like *qatala* (he fought), *qitalan*. Qatada and Shibl, from the people of Mecca, read *wiṭ'an* with a kasra on the waw, a sukun on the ta', and a hamza, shortened (*maqsuran*). Ibn Muhsin read *wa'an* with a fatha on the waw, long (*mamdudan*).

﴿And more upright in speech﴾: that is, and worse in utterance; or more firmly established in recitation, because of the presence of the heart and the quietness of voices. *Qilan* (قيلا) in both cases is a verbal noun, but on the first reading it is general, covering remembrances and supplications, and on the second it is restricted to recitation. Its accusative and the accusative of *wat'an* are as specifications (*tamyiz*, accusative of specification).

Ibn Jarir and others narrated from Anas ibn Malik that he recited "*wa-aswabu qalilan*" (and more correct in a little speech). A man said to him: "We recite it as '*wa-aqwamu qalilan*' (and more upright in a little speech)." He said: "*Asaw'ab*, *aqwam*, and *ahya'* and similar words are all one (in meaning)."

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on Surah 73, verse 7:**

﴿Indeed, for you by day there is extensive occupation.﴾ That is, constant turning about and management of your important affairs, and being busied with your preoccupations, so that you cannot devote yourself fully to worship. Therefore, perform it at night. The origin of *sabh* (swimming, gliding) is the rapid passing through water, and it was then used metaphorically for going in general, as al-Raghib (al-Raghib al-Isfahani) said. They cited the verse of the poet:

*They have permitted you the eastern and western lands, so in them, O friend, there is for you a sabh of sabh.*

This explains the external motive for qiyam al-layl (night prayer), after explaining the motive within the self. It was also said: that is, for you by day there is free time and room for your sleep and for attending to your needs. It was also said: if you miss something of the night, then by day you have free time in which you can make it up. So *sabh* means free time, and this usage is also attested linguistically. However, the first meaning is more consistent with the expression "he swam in the water" and more suitable to the context. Then, this statement is either a completion of the reason, which makes it easier for him that the day is suitable for rest, so let him seize the night for worship, and let him be grateful if he is not obliged to fill both with worship; or it is an emphasis on preserving it, meaning that if it is missed, it must be made up during the day, and there is room for that in the day. This also alludes to the meaning of ﴿He made the night and the day alternating﴾ [al-Furqan: 62].

Ibn Ya'mur, Ikrimah and Ibn Abi Abla read *sabkhan* with the dotted *kha*, meaning the distraction of the heart by preoccupations, borrowed from *sabkh al-suf* (carding of wool), which is the combing out and spreading of its fibres. Many others said it means lightness from obligations. Al-Asma'i said: it is said, "God Almighty lightened the fever from you" (*sabbakha Allahu 'anka al-humma*), meaning He lessened it.

In a hadith: "Do not lighten it with your supplication" (*la tusabbikhi bi-du'a'ik*), meaning, do not lessen it. From the same root is the saying of the poet:

*So lighten your worry, and know that it is so: when the Most Merciful decrees a thing, it will come to pass.*

It was also said that *al-sabkh* means stretching, as it is said, "Stretch out your cotton" (*sabbikhi qutnaki*), meaning stretch it out. The cotton-carding tufts are called *sabā'ikh*, singular *sabkha*. From the same root is the saying of al-Akhtal, describing a hunter and dogs:

*They released them, scattering the dust, as the tufts of cotton are scattered by the bowing of the strings.*

The author of al-Lawami' said: Ibn Ya'mur and Ikrimah, after reading it with the dotted letter, explained *sabkhan* as *nuwwaman*, meaning that one sleeps during the day in order to be helped thereby in standing in prayer at night. This reading may bear other meanings than this, but since they interpreted it this way, we do not go beyond their interpretation. (End of quotation.) Perhaps this is an explanation by a necessary consequence.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 73, verse 8:**

﴿And remember the name of your Lord﴾, meaning: persist in His remembrance, by night and by day, in whatever form it takes, whether glorifying (tasbih), declaring His oneness (tahlil), praising Him (tahmid), prayer (salah), reciting the Qur'an, or other acts. He interpreted the command as one of continuity because he, peace and blessings be upon him, was never forgetful of Him, so that he would need to be commanded to remember Him, glorified be He. The intended continuity is customary (al-dawam al-'urfi), not literal (al-dawam al-haqiqi), because the literal sense is not possible. Also, the context suggests that this is a generalization after a specification, so the meaning, as you have heard, takes into account both night and day.

﴿And devote yourself to Him with complete devotion﴾, meaning: cut yourself off to Him, glorified be He, through worship, strip yourself of everything other than Him, mighty and majestic is He, and immerse yourself in watchfulness over Him, glorified be He. It seems that this is a command concerning what relates to the inner self, after the command concerning what relates to the outer self. To emphasize this, He, glorified be He, said ﴿complete devotion﴾. It is in the accusative (nasb, the grammatical accusative case) by virtue of ﴿devote yourself﴾ (tabattul), because it implicitly contains the meaning of "devote" (battala), as has been said. The discussion of verifying this has already been mentioned at His statement, exalted is He, ﴿And Allah has caused you to grow from the earth as a growth﴾ [Nuh: 17], so recall it. There is an ancient precedent for this matter. Whatever the case, the verse observes the rhyme of the verse endings (al-fawasil).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 73, verse 9:

﴿Lord of the East and the West﴾ is in the nominative (marfu') as a laudatory adjective (madh), and it was also said that it is in the nominative as an inchoative (ibtida', a subject with an elided predicate), its predicate being ﴿there is no god but Him﴾. Zayd ibn 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with them both, read «Rabba» in the accusative (nasb) as a specification (ikhtisas) and praise, and this supports the first reading. Al-Akhawan (Hamza and al-Kisa'i), Ibn 'Amir, Abu Bakr and Ya'qub read «﴿Rabbi﴾» in the genitive (jarr) as a substitute (badal) for ﴿your Lord﴾. It was also said that it is in the genitive by the elision of the particle of oath (harf al-qasam), and its response (jawab) is ﴿there is no god but Him﴾. In this view there is the elision of the particle of oath without anything taking its place and the retention of its governing effect, and this is extremely weak, as explained in the grammar books. This view has been transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, but Abu Hayyan objected to it, saying: "It may not be authentically transmitted from him, because it involves eliding the preposition in an oath, which the Basrans do not permit, except in the noble word of Allah's name, as in 'by Allah, I will surely do such-and-such,' and no analogy may be drawn from it. Also, a negated nominal clause in the response of an oath is negated only with 'ma' and not with 'la illa'; a clause beginning with a present-tense verb is negated with 'la illa' frequently, and with a past-tense verb of similar meaning rarely." End of quotation.

The apparent sense of Ibn Malik's words in al-Tashil is that a negated clause may freely serve as the response of an oath. In his commentary on al-Kafiyah he said that a nominal clause may serve as the response of an oath when it begins with the negating «la», but that it must be repeated if its predicate is placed first or if its subject is definite, as in: "By Allah, there is no man or woman in the house," and "By Allah, Zayd is not in the house, nor is 'Amr." From this it is known that the question is disputed between these two imams.

Ibn 'Abbas, 'Abdullah and their companions read «Lord of the easts and the wests» (rabb al-mashariq wa'l-maghareb), in the plural, and with the dual form as well. The discussion of the reasons for the singular and plural has already been presented.

The fa' in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿so take Him as a trustee﴾, indicates the sequence of the command, and its implication, based on the exclusivity of divinity and lordship to Him, is ('azza wa-jall) and majestic. Wakil is a form (fa'il) in the sense of a passive participle (maf'ul), meaning "one to whom affairs are entrusted." What is meant by taking Him, glorified is He, as a trustee is that one relies upon Him, glorified is He, and entrusts every affair to Him, 'azza wa-jall.

It has been mentioned that the station of tawakkul (complete reliance) is above the station of tabattul (devotion through withdrawal), because it involves the removal of one's own choice. It also indicates the utmost love for Him, exalted is He. They recited:

My passion for Him is an obligation, whether He inclines toward me or turns away,
and His spring is sweet, whether it is clouded or clear.

I have committed all my affair to the Beloved,
so if He wills, He gives me life, and if He wills, He destroys me.

From the sayings of some of the masters: "Whoever is content with Allah, exalted is He, as a trustee, finds a path to every good."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 73, verse 10:

﴿And be patient over what they say﴾, of the fables that pain you, such as their saying that He separates the beloved from his beloved, as you have heard in some of the narrations of the occasions of revelation. ﴿And forsake them with gracious forsaking﴾, by keeping away from them, bearing with them, not repaying them in kind, and entrusting their affairs to their Lord, as is indicated by it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 73, verse 11:

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And leave Me with the deniers﴾ means: leave Me to deal with them and entrust their affair to Me, for in that (there is) what empties your heart (of worry) and clears away your distress. It has already been mentioned that the complete discussion of this is in (its place). Al-Alusi also permitted that, in "the deniers" here, they are the ones who are speaking, so that there is the placing of the apparent noun in the position of the pronoun, and it marks them with the brand of blame, along with an indication of the cause of the threat. He also permitted that they are some of the speakers, so that it means (“leave Me with the deniers”) from among them. It has been said that the verse was revealed concerning the chieftains of Quraysh who mocked (the Prophet), and it has been said concerning those who fed (the poor) on the day of Badr.

﴿Who possess luxury﴾ means: the possessors of ease, pleasant living, abundance of wealth and children. Thus ni‘mah (with a fatha) means ease and comfort; as for ni‘mah (with a kasra) it means bestowal and what one is blessed with; and as for ni‘mah (with a damma) it means joy.

﴿And give them respite for a little﴾ means: a little time, and this is the duration of the life of this world. It has been said that it is the period remaining until the day of Badr. In either case, qalīlan (a little) is in the accusative as an adverb of time (ẓarf). He also permitted that it is in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar), meaning "a little respite." The form tafʿīl (in mahhilhum) is for the intensiveness of the object.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 73, verse 12:

﴿Indeed, with Us are shackles﴾ — plural of nakl, pronounced with a kasra or a fatha on the nun, meaning a heavy fetter; it is also said to mean a strong one. Al-Kalbi said that al-Ankal (the shackles) are iron chains. The first (meaning) is better known in the language. Al-Sha'bi reported: "The shackles are not placed on their feet out of fear of their fleeing, but rather, when they wish to rise, they are pulled down upon them." The sentence is a justification for His saying, ﴿leave Me﴾, and what is conjoined to it; it is as if it were said: Leave their affair to Me, and give them a little respite, because with Me is what I will use to take vengeance upon them, far more severe vengeance: shackles, ﴿and a blazing Fire﴾ — a fire of intense kindling.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 73, verses 13–14:**

﴿And food that chokes﴾, which lodges in the throats and can hardly be swallowed, like the *ḍarīʿ* (a thorny plant) and the *zaqqūm* (a tree of Hell). It is reported from Ibn ʿAbbās: a thorn of fire that stands across their throats, neither coming out nor going down. ﴿And a painful punishment﴾, and another kind of punishment, painful, whose measure no one can estimate and whose reality no one knows except Allah, Mighty and Majestic, as the contrast and the indefiniteness (in the Arabic) indicate. How great is this verse!

Imam Ahmad related it in *al-Zuhd*, Ibn Abi Dawud in *al-Sharīʿa*, Ibn ʿAdi in *al-Kāmil*, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Shuʿab*, by way of Hamran ibn Aʿyan, from Abu Harb ibn al-Aswad: "The Prophet (ﷺ) heard a man reciting ﴿Indeed with Us are fetters﴾ etc., and he fainted (ṣaʿiqa)."

In another narration: "He (ﷺ) himself recited ﴿Indeed with Us are fetters﴾, and when he reached ﴿painful﴾ he fainted."

Khalid ibn Hassan said: al-Hasan spent the evening with us while he was fasting, and I brought him food, but this verse ﴿Indeed with Us﴾ etc. came to him. He said, "Take it away." On the second night I brought him food, and it came to him again, and he said, "Take it away." The same happened on the third night. So his son went to Thabit al-Bunani, Yazid al-Dabbi and Yahya al-Bakka', and told them his story. They came with him and did not stop urging him until he drank a sip of *sawīq* (a barley drink).

If the above hadith is authentic, it provides a justification for the Sufis (mystics) and those like them who swoon upon hearing some verses. The disapproval of ʿĀʾisha, may Allah be pleased with her, and of those who agreed with her, would be left without standing. Unless it is said that the disapproval applies only to one who does this deliberately, and such a person is deserving of being rebuked, as is clear. Or it may be said that *ṣaʿiqa* here is from *al-ṣaʿq* (with the ʿayn sukūn, though it may be vocalised), meaning he was overcome or lost consciousness, and not from *al-ṣaʿaq* (with the ʿayn vocalised), meaning a intense loud sound. This is something ʿĀʾisha, may Allah be pleased with her, and others did not disapprove of.

Al-Imam (Fakhr al-Din al-Razi) has a statement on this verse similar to the statements of the Sufis. He said: Know that it is possible to understand these four levels as spiritual punishment. As for the *ankāl* (fetters), they refer to the soul remaining in the bonds of physical attachments and bodily pleasures. In this world, when it has acquired the habit of that love and desire, then after the body it intensely longs (for them), while the instruments of acquisition have ceased. So those (attachments) become like fetters and shackles preventing it from escaping to the world of spirit and purity. Then from those spiritual shackles spiritual fires are generated, for the intensity of its inclination towards bodily states, and its inability to reach them, produces a severe spiritual burning, like one who desires strongly to obtain something but does not find it, so his heart burns over it. That is the *jaḥīm* (blazing fire). Then it swallows the choking of deprivation and the pain of separation. That is what is meant by His words, Glorified is He, ﴿and food that chokes﴾. Then, because of these states, it remains deprived of the manifestation of the light of Allah, Exalted, and of joining the rank of the holy ones (*al-quddūsiyyīn*). That is what is meant by His words, Mighty and Majestic, ﴿and a painful punishment﴾. The indefiniteness of *ʿadhāban* (a punishment) indicates that it is more intense than what preceded and more complete. Know that I do not say the meaning of the verse is only what I have mentioned, but I say that it gives the four physical levels and the four spiritual levels, and there is no barrier to applying it to both, even if the word is literal in relation to the physical levels and figurative in relation to the spiritual levels, but it is a common and well-known figurative usage. End.

It was objected to this that applying it to both would entail combining the literal and the figurative meanings, or generalising the figurative without a clear indicator, and there is nothing in the speech that points to this in any way. And you know that most of the Sufis' "allusions" (*ishāra*) are of this kind.

His words, Exalted is He, ﴿The earth and the mountains will quake﴾ — it has been said that it is connected to *dharnī* (leave me), and it has been said that it is an attribute of *ʿadhāban* (a punishment), and it has been said that it is connected to *alīman* (painful). A group chose that it is connected to the *istiqrār* (settledness) that *ladaynā* (with Us) is connected to, meaning: that punishment is settled with Us and manifests on the day when the earth and the mountains shake and tremble. Zayd ibn ʿAlī recited *tarjufu* (will quake) in the passive voice. ﴿And the mountains were﴾, despite their firmness and height, ﴿a heap of sand﴾, a gathered mass of sand, from *kathaba al-shayʾ* when he gathered it. It is as if in origin it was *faʿīl* in the sense of *mafʿūl*, then it became dominant until it took the rule of solid nouns. The statement is on the basis of an eloquent simile. It has been said that there is no barrier to its being literal sand. ﴿Crumbling﴾: it has been said that it means soft and loose, so when a foot treads on it, it slips away from beneath it. It has also been said that it means scattered, from *hīla* (to be poured), when it is scattered and poured out. Its being called "a heap" is with regard to what it was before scattering, so there is no contradiction between being gathered and being scattered. The intended meaning is not that it is in the state of that or on the verge of it, as has been said.
