Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 73, verse 15:

﴿Indeed, We have sent to you﴾ is an address to the deniers, the people of luxury (ulu al-ni'mah); whether they are taken to be the speakers or some of them are, there is here an iltifat (shift) from the third person (al-ghaybah), and it is an iltifat of great significance. That is: Indeed, We have sent to you, O deniers from among the people of Makkah, ﴿a messenger as a witness against you﴾, who will bear witness on the Day of Resurrection to what came forth from you of disbelief and disobedience, ﴿as We sent to Pharaoh a messenger﴾, who is Musa, peace be upon him. The non-specification of him is because he is not part of the comparison, or because he is well known and needs no clarification.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 73, verse 16:

﴿But Pharaoh disobeyed the Messenger﴾, the one mentioned, whom We had sent to him. The definite article is for the anaphoric reference (al-'ahd al-dhikri, the definiteness of a previously mentioned referent), and the kaf is in the accusative position, as an attribute (sifah) of a deleted verbal noun (masdar) on the assumption that it is a noun, meaning: a sending like Our sending. Or the prepositional phrase is in the position of an attribute, on the assumption that the kaf is a particle, meaning: a sending existing as. The meaning is: We sent to you a messenger as a witness over you, and you disobeyed him, just as We sent to Pharaoh a messenger and he disobeyed him. Repeating Pharaoh and the Messenger as explicit nouns serves to magnify the gravity of his disobedience, and this is because it was disobedience to the Messenger, not because it was disobedience to Moses. In this there is that the disobedience of those addressed is more grievous and more deeply rooted in blame, since the Exalted, Majestic One added for this Messenger another attribute, namely ﴿a witness over you﴾, and incorporated within it that if they had believed, the testimony would have been in their favor. As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿So We seized him with a heavy seizing﴾, wabil means heavy, of poor outcome, from their saying "kala' wabil" (a grievous pasture), and "hamm la yustamra'" (a fever that cannot be digested) because of its heaviness. Al-wabil also means a large staff, and from it comes al-wabil (heavy rain) for a heavy, large downpour. The expression is outside the realm of simile; it was brought to inform those addressed that they are seized with the like of that, and more severe, and more severe.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 73, verse 17:

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿How, then, will you guard yourselves, if you disbelieve, against a Day that will make children grey-haired?﴾ is a sequence of ranks, following on from ﴿as We sent a messenger to Pharaoh﴾ (in the sense of the disobedience). "A day" (yawman) is the direct object of "you guard against" (tattaqūna). It is either with an elided modifier, i.e. "the punishment of a day" or "the terror of a day," or without it. (illā) The meaning is according to this, and the pronoun in "makes" (yaj'alu) refers to the day, and the clause is its attribute, and the attribution is metaphorical. Some have said the pronoun refers to God, Exalted is He, and the attribution is literal, and the clause is an attribute with its connecting pronoun elided, i.e. "He makes [children grey-haired] in it," as in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And guard yourselves against a day when no soul will avail another﴾ [al-Baqarah: 48]. The apparent order would have been for this to precede His saying ﴿as We sent﴾, but it was delayed until here, as an increase upon an increase in awe-inspiring terror. It is as if it were said: suppose you are not seized in this world with the seizure of Pharaoh and his like, how will you guard your souls against the terror of the Resurrection and what has been prepared for you of shackles, if you persist in what you are upon and die in disbelief? As for His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿if you disbelieve﴾, its estimation is that of something whose existence is doubted, which draws attention to the fact that, with the sending of this Messenger, no one should have any doubt remaining that keeps him in disbelief; thus he is the clear light.

It is also permissible that "a day" be an adverbial complement of "you guard" (tattaqūna), in the sense of: how, then, will you have taqwa on the Day of Resurrection, if you disbelieve in this world? The speech in that case is an exhortation to desist from disbelief and a warning against the like of the fate of the family of Pharaoh before regret will no longer benefit. It is also permissible that it be governed by "you disbelieve" (kafartum) with the interpretation "you denied" (jahadtum), and the meaning: how is there hope for your desisting from disbelief and for guarding against God, Exalted is He, and fearing Him, while you deny the Day of Recompense? It is as if, when it was said "a day when the earth will quake," He followed it with His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿how, then, will you guard yourselves﴾ against God if you disbelieve in Him; so the mention of the day is repeated with another attribute, as an increase in terror. The first aspect is preferable; so said al-Kashshaf. Al-Allamah al-Tibi said, regarding the last aspect, namely the governing of "a day" by "you disbelieve," that it is more harmonious with the composition, meaning: We warned you with shackles and blazing fire, and We sent to you a messenger as a witness on the Day of Resurrection against your disbelief and denial, and We warned you with what We did to Pharaoh of severe punishment and heavy seizure; yet none of that took effect upon you, nor did you fear God, Exalted is He; so how will you guard against Him and fear Him if you deny the Day of Resurrection and Recompense? In this there is the point that the essence of taqwa and fear is faith in the Day of Resurrection. End.

It is not hidden that the eloquence of the meaning favours the first aspect. A group went to the view that the address in ﴿Indeed We have sent to you﴾ is general, to the black and the red; so the apparent reading is that it is not a shift of address at all. Whatever the case, "making children grey-haired" means "making them shuyūkh (elders)," the plural of ashyab. It has been said it is literal: children turn grey and their hair whitens from the severity of the Day of Resurrection. This is in line with what Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn Mas'ud: "When God says to Adam, peace be upon him, 'Arise and bring forth from your offspring the portion for the Fire,' he says, 'O Lord, I have no knowledge except what You have taught me.' God, Mighty and Majestic, says, 'Bring forth the portion for the Fire: from every thousand, nine hundred and ninety-nine.' They will come forth and be driven to the Fire in a driven throng, blue-eyed, with grim faces." Ibn Mas'ud said: "When the portion for the Fire comes forth, every child turns grey."

In the hadith of al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh from Ibn 'Abbas: "We are that." It has also been said it is a figure for the intensity of terror, without there being actual greying, for they say of a severe day: "a day that makes the forelocks of children grey." The origin of this is that when worries pile up upon a man they weaken his strength and hasten greyness in him; hence it was said: greyness is the blossom of worries. The hadith of the resurrection does not reject this. Al-Zamakhshari allowed that this is a description of the day as long, and that children reach old age in it; or that senility and greyness are meant, not an actual estimate, but a description of its length only, according to what people are accustomed to; otherwise it is longer than that and longer still, so there is no objection. Yet with this he is not wholly satisfied. The apparent reading is the generality of "children." al-Suddi said that the "children" here are children of fornication. It has been said they are the children of polytheists. Zayd ibn 'Ali read "yawma" without tanwin and "najʻalu" with the nun, so the adverb is then construed as a genitive before the clause "najʻalu," and so on.

[p. 110]

﴿The sky will be split apart﴾, meaning it will be cracked open. It was also read as «mutafarriṭ», meaning cracking and splitting. ﴿Because of it﴾, meaning because of that Day. The bāʾ here is the bāʾ of instrumentality (ʾālah), like in your saying, "I split the wood with the axe, so it split because of it." The meaning is that the sky, despite its magnitude and firmness, will split apart from the intensity and terror of that Day, just as a thing splits by that which splits it. So what do you suppose about other creatures? It is also permissible that the meaning is that the sky is now weighed down by it, with a weight that leads to its splitting, because of its greatness upon it and its fear of its occurrence, like His saying, exalted is He, ﴿It weighs heavily upon the heavens﴾ (al-Aʿrāf: 187). The speech is then of the type of imaginative depiction (takhyīl), and the splitting is a metonymy (kināyah) for the extreme heaviness of that Day. The purpose is to convey that it is now in this condition. The first interpretation is more apparent and more consistent with most of the verses.

It seems that the apparent form would be "the sky is splitting" (muntafiṭah) with a feminine predicate, because it is well known that "the sky" (al-samāʾ) is feminine. However, it was considered appropriate to treat it as a masculine described noun, so it was made masculine: meaning "a thing that splits by it." The point in this is to alert that its reality has changed, its name and its form have departed from it, and nothing remains of it except what is expressed as "a thing" (shayʾ).

Abū ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ, Abū ʿUbayda, and al-Kisāʾī, and those who followed them, including Mundhir ibn Saʿīd, said the masculine form is due to interpreting "the sky" as "the ceiling" (saqf). The point in this is to bring to mind the sense of a ceiling and its collapse, so that the matter of splitting would be more astonishing and terrifying. Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī said the implied meaning is "one possessing splitting" (dhāt infiṭār), like their saying "a nursing woman" (mursiʿ), meaning "one possessing nursing" (dhāt riḍāʿ), so it proceeded in the manner of a relative adjective (nisbah). It is also reported from him that this is of the type of "locusts scattered" (al-jarād al-muntashir), "green trees" (al-shajar al-akhḍar), and "the trunks of uprooted palm trees" (aʿjāz nakhlin munqaʿir). That is, the sky belongs to the category of collective nouns (ism al-jins) which, between it and its singular, there is a feminine marker (tāʾ al-taʾnīth). Its singular is samāʾah, and a collective noun may be treated as either masculine or feminine, so "munfaṭir" came in the masculine.

Al-Farrāʾ said: "al-samāʾ," meaning the canopy, may be masculine or feminine, so "munfaṭir" came in the masculine. From this is the saying of the poet:

"If He were to raise the sky to Him by pillars, we would be lifted up with the sky and with the clouds."

According to this, there is no need for interpretation. Rather, what is sought is the point of treating it as masculine, although most usage treats it as feminine. Its point is probably evident to anyone with a little understanding.

Interpreting the bāʾ in ﴿bihi﴾ as instrumental is the most fitting for magnifying the matter of that Day. It is also permissible to interpret it as temporal (ẓarfiyyah), meaning "the sky splits within it." The return of the pronoun in the genitive case to the Day is the apparent view on which the majority agree. Mujāhid said it returns to God, exalted is He, meaning by His command, glory be to Him, and His authority, mighty and majestic is He. So it is, in his view, like the pronoun in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿His promise was ever to be fulfilled﴾, since it refers to God, exalted is He, as is known from the context. The verbal noun is then added to its agent. It is also permissible that it refers to the Day, like the pronoun in "bihi" according to the majority, and the verbal noun is then added to its object.

This is the commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 73, verse 19:

﴿Indeed, this﴾ is a reference to the verses containing the calamities mentioned, ﴿is a reminder﴾, i.e., an admonition, ﴿so whoever wills may take to his Lord a way﴾ by drawing near to Him, exalted is He, through faith and obedience, for that is the path (minhaj) that leads to His good pleasure, mighty and majestic is He. The object of ﴿wills﴾ is omitted, and the usual practice in such cases is to supply it from the same kind as the response (jawab), i.e., "whoever wills to take a way to his Lord, exalted is He, takes [it]," and so on. Some have supplied it as "the taking of admonition," in keeping with what precedes it, i.e., "whoever wills to take admonition, ﴿takes to his Lord a way﴾." The intended meaning is that whoever intends to attain admonition draws near to Him, exalted is He; but the cause has been mentioned while its effect is intended, so this is in reality the recompense. Al-Bahr (al-Bahr al-Muhit, by Abu Hayyan) chose the more well-known reading, and said that the statement is in the sense of promise and threat (wa'd wa wa'id).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 73, verse 20 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Indeed, your Lord knows that you stand (in prayer) for less than two-thirds of the night﴾. That is, for a time less than the two-thirds. Here *adna* is used, which is the superlative of *dana* (to be near), meaning "nearer" or "less," because when the distance between two things is near, the space between them is small. So it is a metonymy of the figurative kind (*majaz mursal*), since nearness entails a small space between two things, and the word is used for its consequence, or for the general notion of smallness. It is also permitted to take it as a comparison between nearness and smallness, so that there is a metaphor (*isti'ara*), but the metonymy is closer to the meaning.

Al-Hasan, Shayba, Abu Haywa, Ibn al-Sumayfa, Hisham, and Ibn Mujahid (on the authority of Qunbul), as the author of *al-Kamil* reported, read *thuluthay* with a sukun on the lam. This is also reported from Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir, as the author of *al-Lawami'* reported.

﴿And half of it, and a third of it﴾, in the accusative, as a conjunction with *adna*. It is as if it were said: "He knows that you stand for less than two-thirds of the night, and you stand for half of it, and you stand for a third of it." Al-'Arabiyyan (Abu 'Amr and al-Kisa'i) and Nafi' read *wa-nisfihi wa-thuluthihi* in the genitive, as a conjunction with *thuluthay al-layl*. That is, "you stand for less than two-thirds, less than half, and less than a third." The first reading corresponds to the option, mentioned earlier, between standing for half in full, standing for less than half, which is a third, and standing for more than half, which is the nearer part of two-thirds. The second reading corresponds to the option between half, which is nearer than two-thirds, and a third, which is nearer than half, and a quarter, which is nearer than a third. So said more than one scholar, so do not overlook this. The matter has been raised as an objection: the difference between the two readings is evident, so how is the soundness of God's knowledge reconciled with their meanings, since they cannot be combined? The answer given is that this is according to the times: each occurred at a particular time, so both were known to God, the Exalted.

This point has also been raised as an objection, on the assumption that the command was addressed to the greater portion. It would then follow either that the Prophet (ﷺ) contravened what he was commanded, or that he exercised ijtihad and erred in conforming to the command. Both are invalid.

The first is evident, especially if the command is for obligation. As for the second, whoever permits the Prophet's ijtihad and his error in it says that he (peace be upon him) would not have been left to persist in an error. The answer given is to accept that the command was addressed to the lesser portion, but they added extra, out of caution against falling into contravention, and it would have been difficult for them. God, glory be to Him, knew that if they did not take the more difficult course they would fall into contravention, so He abrogated the command. So it has been said, but reflect on it, for the matter still needs consideration.

Ibn Kathir, in the transmission of Shibl, read *wa-thuluthahu* with a sukun on the lam.

﴿And a group of those with you﴾: this is a conjunction with the hidden pronoun in *taqum* (you stand), and the separation between them makes it acceptable. That is, "a group of your companions stands with you."

﴿And God measures the night and the day﴾: He does not know the exact measures of their hours as they are, except God, the Exalted. The placing of His name first as the subject, followed by the predicate *yuqaddiru* (measures), indicates exclusivity (*ikhtisas*), according to what al-Zamakhshari (Jar Allah) held. This is supported by God's words: ﴿He knew that you could not keep count of it﴾. The pronoun refers to an understood verbal noun (*masdar*), not to the standing mentioned in the discourse. The meaning is: "He knew that the matter is that you will not be able to measure the times, nor be able to master the hours, nor will it be possible for you to calculate them by equal and balanced division, except that you take the wider course out of caution. That is burdensome for you and reaches you."

﴿So He turned to you [in forgiveness]﴾: that is, by granting the concession to abandon the prescribed standing and by lifting the responsibility from you for abandoning it. The expression is a metaphor, in which the granting of concession is likened to the acceptance of repentance in lifting responsibility. The common word, used for the thing compared to, is employed for the thing compared, as in God's words: ﴿So He turned to you and pardoned you. So now, have relations with them﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:187). Some claimed that it is to be taken in its apparent sense, and said that this shows that some of them had left part of what they were commanded. This is not correct.

﴿So recite of the Qur'an what is easy for you﴾: that is, pray what is easy for you of the night prayer. He expressed the prayer by the recitation, just as He expressed it by its other pillars. It has also been said that the speech is to be taken in its literal sense, as a demand to recite the Qur'an itself, but this is remote from the context. Whoever holds the first view says that God prescribed the standing for a specific amount of the night in His words: ﴿Stand [in prayer] the night﴾, and so on. Then He abrogated it by standing for some amount of it, in His words: ﴿So He turned to you. So recite﴾, and so on. The command in both places is for obligation, except that the obligation at first was a specific one among specific amounts, and afterward was an unspecified part. Then the obligation of standing upon the community in general was abrogated by the five daily prayers.

Whoever holds the second view says that God granted them a concession to abandon standing entirely, and commanded them to recite some of the Qur'an at night. It is as if it were said: "He turned to you and granted the concession to abandon [standing]. If standing is difficult for you, then recite what is easy of the Qur'an, for this is not difficult, and by this recitation you will attain the reward of standing." A group has stated explicitly that on this view the *faqra'u* is a command of recommendation (*nadb*), whereas on the first view it is obligatory.

Know that they differed concerning the matter of *tahajjud* (night prayer). According to Muqatil and Ibn Kaysan, it was obligatory in Mecca before the five daily prayers were prescribed, and then it was abrogated by them, except for what they performed voluntarily. This is narrated by al-Bukhari and Muslim in the hadith of Jabir. Imam Ahmad, Muslim, Abu Dawud, al-Darimi, Ibn Majah, and al-Nasa'i narrated, from Sa'd ibn Hisham, who said: "I said to 'A'isha: 'O Mother of the Believers, inform me about the character of the Messenger of God (ﷺ).' She said: 'Do you not recite the Qur'an?' I said: 'Yes.' She said: 'The character of the Prophet of God is the Qur'an.' He said: 'I resolved to stand and not ask anyone about anything until I die. Then it occurred to me, and I said: "Inform me about the standing of the Messenger of God (ﷺ)." She said: "Do you not recite: O you wrapped in garments?" I said: "Yes." She said: "God, the Exalted, made the night standing obligatory at the beginning of this surah. So the Prophet of God and his companions stood for a year, and God held back its conclusion for twelve months in the heaven, until God, the Exalted, sent down the lightening at the end of the surah, and the night standing became voluntary.'"

In another narration from her, it continued for eight months. From Qatada: it continued for a year or two. From some of them: it was obligatory, and the option was only regarding the amount, and then it was abrogated after ten years. The man, as al-Kalbi said, would stand until morning, out of fear that he would not be able to keep count of the portion between half, a third, and two-thirds. It has also been said that it was a supererogatory prayer (*nafl*), as evidenced by the option regarding the amount and by God's words: ﴿And from the night, perform tahajjud with it as a supererogatory act for you﴾ (al-Isra' 17:79). More than one scholar reported this, and they discussed it. However, Imam, the author of *al-Kashf*, said: this speaker did not intend that the option negates obligation. Rather, he argued by induction, that obligatory acts have fixed times, whether wide or narrow, and the determination of these is not left to the judgment of the one who performs them. This is a sound argument.

As for the one who holds the obligatory view, he looked at the wording without considering external evidence. Each has a basis. As for his statement, "and based on God's words: ﴿And from the night﴾," the argument is that the verse explains ﴿as a supererogatory act for you﴾ as meaning "additional to the obligatory prayers, specifically for you, and not for others, because it is voluntary for them." This speaker does not deny that it is obligatory for the Prophet (peace be upon him), but he denies it for others besides him (ﷺ). The verse indicates this, so there is no need to consider it.

Furthermore, when God, glory be to Him, mentioned in that surah ﴿and from the night﴾, meaning that He specified part of the night without a fixed time, here He fixed the time, may He be exalted, and indicated the participation of the community with him (peace be upon him) in His words: ﴿and a group of those with you﴾. Then what was revealed there was for obligation upon him (ﷺ) alone, while here it is for voluntary observance for him and for the community. This is a sound view. Yet God's words, ﴿He knew that you could not keep count of it, so He turned to you﴾, support the first view. End of quotation. By the first view he meant the view of obligation for him (peace be upon him) and for the community. The numerous reports of the narrations bear witness to it. However, in *al-Bahr* it is stated that God's words, ﴿and a group of those with you﴾, are evidence that it was not obligatory upon all. For if it were obligatory upon them, the phrasing would be ﴿and those with you﴾. Unless one holds that among them were some who stood in their homes and some who stood with him, in which case it is possible that the obligation applied to all at that time. End of quotation. You know that the *min* here is not necessarily partitive; it may be explanatory. Those who hold the view of obligation for all began by interpreting it that way, not as partitive on account of the companionship, for that is not what it means. And God, the Exalted, knows best.

On the last view, the verse, in His words, ﴿So recite﴾, and so on, indicates the recommendation of reciting some of the Qur'an at night. In some reports: "Whoever recites a hundred verses in a night, the Qur'an will not argue against him." In some: "Whoever recites a hundred verses is written among the devout (*qanitin*)." In some: fifty verses. The more reliable of the two views on this is the first, and you have heard that the command on it is for obligation, and that the standing of some part of the night was obligatory, then its obligation was abrogated for the community by the obligation of the five daily prayers. So today, for the community, it is a sunnah.

In *al-Bahr*, after explaining ﴿so recite﴾ as "pray," and after quoting what was said about abrogation, it is stated: this command, according to the majority, is a command of permission (*ibahah*). Al-Hasan and Ibn Sirin said: standing in the night is obligatory, even for the time it takes to milk a sheep. Ibn Jubayr and a group said: it is obligatory without which one cannot do, even for fifty verses. End of quotation.

The apparent context of this indicates that these scholars hold that it is obligatory today, and that it did not abrogate the obligation absolutely, but only abrogated the obligation of a specific portion. This is contrary to what is well known. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas that the standing of the night was dropped for the companions of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and became voluntary, while it remained obligatory upon the Messenger of God (peace be upon him). I think the matter needs no proof. So let us fold up the carpet of speculation and argument. Yes, the righteous predecessors (*al-salaf al-salih*) persevered in standing as they persevered in the obligations of Islam, because of what it contains of solitude with the Beloved and intimacy with Him, and He is near without a watcher. We ask God, the Exalted, to grant us success as He granted them success, and to bestow His favor upon us as He bestowed it upon them.

A matter remains here. Imam Abu Hanifa, may God be pleased with him, argued from God's words, ﴿So recite of the Qur'an what is easy for you﴾, that the obligatory part of the prayer is the recitation in general, not specifically the Fatihah. This is clear if one holds that the verse expresses the prayer by its pillar, which is recitation, just as it expresses it by prostration, standing, and bowing in other places. He estimated "what is easy" as one verse, according to what al-Mawardi reported from him, and as a third (of the Qur'an), according to what Ibn al-'Arabi reported from him. The question is established in the books of jurisprudence (*furu'*).

Al-Shafi'i and Malik restricted "what is easy" to the Fatihah. They argued for the obligation of reciting it in prayer with many proofs. Among them is what Abu Hamid al-Isfara'ini narrated from Ibn al-Mundhir, with his chain, from Abu Hurayra, from the Prophet (ﷺ): "No prayer is valid in which the Opening of the Book (al-Fatihah) is not recited."

Among them also is what was narrated, likewise, from Abu Hurayra, from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Every prayer in which the Opening of the Book is not recited is *khidaj*, it is *khidaj*." That is, it is deficient, or it is one with deficiency, for emphasis. It was objected that deficiency does not indicate that it is impermissible. The answer is that it does indicate this, because the obligation of prayer remains in place, and the original state of what is established is continuance. We depart from this when the prayer is performed in its complete form, so when it is deficient it must remain on the original state and not be released from the obligation.

It is reinforced by the view of Abu Hanifa that it is not permissible to fast on the day of 'Id as a make-up for Ramadan, even though the fast on that day is valid according to him. He argues that what is obligatory is the complete fast, and fasting on this day is deficient, so it does not free one from the obligation.

Among them also is his (ﷺ) statement: "There is no prayer except with the Opening of the Book."

[Page 113]

It is clear in the intended meaning, since the implied sense is "there is no valid prayer without it." It was objected that the intended meaning could be "there is no complete prayer without it." Since negating the very existence of prayer is impossible, because prayer exists without al-Fatiha, it becomes necessary to direct the negation to one of prayer's rulings. Directing it to validity is no more appropriate than directing it to completeness.

It is answered that we do not concede the impossibility of negating the prayer's essence. If al-Fatiha is a part of the reality (*mahiyyah*) of prayer, then the reality is negated when it is not recited, so negating its essence is valid. The impossibility would only hold if it were established that al-Fatiha is not a part of prayer, and that is the very point at issue. Even granting this, we do not concede that directing the negation to validity is no more appropriate than directing it to completeness. Rather, validity is more appropriate, because resorting to the closest figurative meaning when the literal meaning is impossible is preferable, indeed obligatory by *ijma'* (scholarly consensus). There is no doubt that an existing thing which is not valid is closer to non-existence than an existing thing which is complete. Also, the original state of affairs (*al-asl*) is that what was established remains, and that is the obligation (*taklif*) as it was. Also, the side of prohibition (*hurmah*) is weightier, because it is more cautious. Also, performing prayer without al-Fatiha entails losing an additional excellence without necessity, since there is *ijma'* that prayer with it is more excellent. Therefore it is not permissible to go to that, because it is ugly by custom, and so it is ugly by the Law, based on his saying ﷺ: "What the Muslims consider good is good with Allah, and what the Muslims consider ugly is ugly with Allah."

Also, its recitation entails escaping the obligation with certainty, so it is more cautious. Therefore it is required to affirm its obligation, based on the text: "Leave what makes you doubt for what does not make you doubt."

And from reason: averting the harm of fear from oneself, which is obligatory. The belief in obligation producing fear, because we may be mistaken, is opposed by the belief in its non-obligation, so the two counterbalance each other. But in action, recitation does not produce fear, while abandoning it does, so the more cautious course is recitation.

The Hanafis answered with what they answered.

The Hanafis argued that what is obligatory is whatever is easy of the Qur'an, not al-Fatiha specifically, with several proofs, among them what Abu Uthman al-Nahdi narrated from Abu Hurayra, who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ commanded me to go out and proclaim: there is no prayer without recitation, even if it be of the Opening of the Book (al-Fatiha)."

It was countered that this is contradicted by what is reported from Abu Hurayra, who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ commanded me to go out and proclaim: there is no prayer except with the Opening of the Book."

And also that the phrase "even if it be of the Opening of the Book" may mean that if one recites only al-Fatiha it suffices, and this reading must be adopted to harmonize the evidences, though it is a forced interpretation. Perhaps the first answer is that the intended meaning of "even if it be of the Opening of the Book" could be what comes first to understanding from the saying of one who says: "There is no life except with food, even if it be bread, a ration each day," meaning that this amount is indispensable. On this reading the hadith becomes one of the proofs of obligation.

Also, if al-Fatiha were obligatory, then our statement "whenever recitation is obligatory, al-Fatiha is obligatory" would be true. Its meaning is a true premise: if al-Fatiha were not obligatory, then recitation would be obligatory, since the obligation of recitation in general is established by *ijma'*. Thus the two premises yield: if al-Fatiha is not obligatory, then al-Fatiha is obligatory, which is false.

It is answered by rejecting the minor premise, that is, we do not concede the truth of our statement "if al-Fatiha were not obligatory, recitation would be obligatory," because the non-obligation of al-Fatiha is impossible, and an impossibility may entail an impossibility, namely the removal of the obligation of recitation in general, which is established by *ijma'*. Even if we concede it, we do not concede the impossibility of our statement "if al-Fatiha were not obligatory, al-Fatiha would be obligatory," for the reason mentioned just above.

Some used analogy (*qiyas*) as a proof against the Hanafis, arguing that whatever its non-existence entails the existence of, its existence is established necessarily. It was rejected: this holds only if the implication, namely "if al-Fatiha were not obligatory, it would be obligatory," were established in the actual state of affairs, but it is not so; rather it holds on the assumption that reciting al-Fatiha is obligatory. Therefore it does not become a proof against them. The full discussion of this belongs in its proper place.

And you know that on the second opinion regarding the verse, the argument from it for the obligation of recitation in general in prayer does not appear, since there is in it, on that view, nothing more than a command to recite whatever of the Qur'an, little or much, in place of what was enjoined upon them of the night prayer. So let this be noted.

[Page 114]

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He knows that there will be among you those who are ill﴾ is a new sentence (*isti'naf*) explaining another wisdom, other than what was previously mentioned, namely the difficulty of calculating the measure of the times, which calls for concession and lightening. That is: He knows that the matter will be that among you there are ill people ﴿and others who travel through the land﴾ journeying in it for trade ﴿seeking of Allah's bounty﴾, which is profit. He has generalized the seeking of bounty to include acquiring knowledge. The clause is in the position of a circumstantial phrase (*hal*). ﴿And others who fight in the way of Allah﴾, meaning the holy warriors. The pairing of travelers seeking Allah's bounty with them indicates that they are like them in reward.

Sa'id ibn Mansur and al-Bayhaqi in *Shu'ab al-Iman*, and others, reported from Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "There is no state in which death comes to me after striving in the way of Allah that I love more than that it come to me while I am between the two sides of a mountain seeking Allah's bounty," and he recited this verse: ﴿And others travel...﴾ and so on.

Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "There is no importer who brings food to a city of the cities of the Muslims and sells it at the price of its day, except that his station is with Allah." Then the Messenger of Allah ﷺ recited: ﴿And others travel through the land seeking of Allah's bounty, and others fight in the way of Allah﴾.

The meaning is that He, mighty and majestic, knew that there would be among the believers those for whom standing in prayer is hard, just as He knew, glorified is He, the difficulty of calculating the measure of the times. Since the matter is as mentioned, and the requirements of concession have combined, ﴿so recite what is easy of it﴾, that is, of the Qur'an, without bearing hardships. ﴿And establish prayer﴾, that is, the obligatory prayer, ﴿and give zakat﴾, likewise. Most exegetes hold this view, and the apparent meaning is that by the obligatory prayer they meant the five daily prayers, and by the obligatory zakat its well-known counterpart.

It was raised as a difficulty that the surah is among the first revealed at Mecca, and the five prayers were not made obligatory until after the Night Journey (*Isra'*), while zakat was made obligatory only at Medina. It is answered that whoever holds this view must consider these verses to be Medinan. It has also been said that zakat was made obligatory at Mecca in general terms without specifying the shares, and what was made obligatory at Medina was the specifying of the shares, so the zakat meant may be the zakat made obligatory in general, and there is no barrier to the verses being Meccan. But this entails that they were revealed after the Night Journey, and their ruling on the night prayer, which was previously obligatory, conflicts with the concession. It has also been said that the verse may be one whose ruling was delayed after its revelation, but this is not sound.

﴿And lend to Allah a goodly loan﴾ is intended to mean expenditures in the ways of good, or paying zakat in the best and most beneficial manner to the poor.

﴿And whatever good you send forward for yourselves﴾, that is, any good, whether of what was mentioned or of what was not mentioned, ﴿you will find it with Allah, better and greater in reward﴾, that is, than what you postpone until bequest at death. ("Better," *khayran*) is the second object of ("you will find it," *tajiduhu*). It is an emphatic (*ta'kid*) of the pronoun in ("you will find it," *tajiduhu*), even though it has the form of a nominative, because the emphatic is accusative, since *huwa* is used to emphasize the genitive and accusative, as al-Radi mentioned. Or it is a pronoun of separation (*damir al-fasl*), even though it does not occur between two definites, since the elative (*af'al*) has the status of the definite, which is why it refuses the definite article, as with proper nouns. Abu al-Baqa' allowed it to be an apposition (*badal*) from the pronoun in ("you will find it," *tajiduhu*), but Abu Hayyan considered this a mistake, since the obligation falls on it, not on it being the thing itself. Abu al-Sammal read it with *lam*, al-Adawi; Abu al-Simak read it with *kaf*, al-Ghanawi; and Abu al-Sumayfa' read *huwa khayrun wa a'zamu*, with both in the nominative, as the subject and predicate, and the clause is in the position of the second object. Abu Zayd said this is the dialect of the Banu Tamim, who put in the nominative what follows the separating pronoun. They say: *kana Zaydun huwa al-fa'il* with nominative. Upon this is the verse of Qays ibn Dharih:

You long for Lubna, though you have abandoned her,
and you were over her in the assembly, and you are more capable.

Abu 'Amr al-Jirmi said that Sibawayh recited it as evidence for the nominative, and the rhyme is nominative, though it is reported as *aqdara* (accusative).

﴿And seek forgiveness from Allah﴾ in all your states, for a person rarely escapes from what counts as negligence on his part. The Sufis counted among this the seeing of one's own worship by the worshipper. It has been said that for this reason the command to seek forgiveness comes after the earlier commands to establish prayer, give zakat, and lend the goodly loan.

[Page 115]

﴿Indeed Allah is Forgiving, Merciful﴾, so He, glorified is He, forgives the sin of whoever seeks His forgiveness, and has mercy on him, mighty and majestic is He. The omission of the object indicates generality, and the detailed discussion of this is known.

We ask Allah, exalted is He, for His great forgiveness and mercy for us, our parents, and all the believers of His creation, by the sanctity of the master of His creation and the support of the people of His elect, ﷺ, and his companions and followers.
